column2: Cut the pepper into thin strips, the mushrooms into thin slices and the olives into rings.
Place the lavash on the tray and spread the tomato sauce, leaving a 1 cm border.
Sprinkle on half the cheese, then scatter the vegetables and olives over it.
Sprinkle over the remaining cheese and the thyme.
Bake for 8–10 minutes, until the edges are golden and the cheese has melted.
Let it rest for a minute, then slice.
Lavash is thin, so keep an eye on the oven; it browns quickly.
Children can decorate their own pizzas; sweetcorn and boiled chicken also work well.
Serve hot with ayran or a green salad.
Eat fresh; keep leftovers 1 day in the fridge and reheat in a pan.
Pan-fried potatoes with mince
Peel the potatoes and cut into 1.5 cm cubes; finely chop the onion and pepper.
Heat the oil in a wide pan and fry the potatoes for 8 minutes until lightly browned at the edges, then set aside on a plate.
In the same pan, fry the mince for 6–7 minutes until its liquid has cooked off and it has changed colour completely.
Add the onion and pepper and fry for 3 more minutes; add the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute.
Return the potatoes and add the hot water, salt and chilli flakes.
Cook covered over low heat for 12–15 minutes until the potatoes are tender.
Mince must not stay pink inside; cook it through, especially for children and pregnant women.
Frying the potatoes first keeps them from falling apart.
Serve with rice or bulgur pilaf and yoghurt.
One-pot creamy chicken pasta
300 g penne
Dice the chicken small, finely chop the onion and garlic; slice the mushrooms.
Heat the butter and oil in a wide pot and sauté the chicken for 6 minutes until completely white.
Add the onion, garlic and mushrooms and cook for 5 minutes until the mushroom liquid evaporates.
Add the uncooked pasta, hot water and salt and bring to the boil.
Cook for 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the pasta is tender and the water has reduced.
Add the milk and boil for 2 minutes; take off the heat and stir in the cheese until melted.
Stir often so the pasta doesn’t stick to the bottom.
If the sauce is too thick, add a few spoonfuls of hot water.
Serve hot, sprinkled with black pepper and parsley.
Sautéed spinach with chickpeas
Wash the spinach several times in plenty of water and chop roughly.
Chop the onion finely and the garlic even more finely.
Heat the olive oil in a wide pan, soften the onion for 4 minutes, add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the chickpeas and cumin and fry for 2 minutes.
Add the spinach and cook for 4–5 minutes, stirring as it wilts.
Add the salt, take off the heat and squeeze over the lemon juice.
If the spinach releases a lot of water, raise the heat briefly to evaporate it.
Add the lemon juice last to boost iron absorption.
Serve with garlic yoghurt and wholemeal bread.
Omelette with curd cheese and dill
3 sprigs of dill
Finely chop the dill.
Beat the eggs with the milk; add the curd cheese, dill and pepper and mix.
Melt the butter in the pan over medium heat and pour in the mixture.
When the edges start to set, push them towards the centre with a spatula so the raw egg runs underneath.
Cook for 3–4 minutes until the top is no longer runny and fully cooked, then fold in half and remove.
If the curd cheese is unsalted, you can add a pinch of salt.
In pregnancy, make sure the egg is fully cooked.
Serve with tomatoes and wholemeal bread.
Homemade ayran
2 cups cold drinking water
A few fresh mint leaves (optional)
Put the yoghurt in a large jug.
Add the salt and whisk the yoghurt until smooth.
Keep whisking while you add the cold water little by little.
Blend with a stick blender for 30 seconds to make it frothy.
Garnish with mint leaves if you like and serve cold.
Adjust the consistency to taste with the amount of water.
You can reduce the salt or leave it out altogether.
Serve cold straight away.
Keeps 1 day in a closed bottle in the fridge; shake before drinking.
